title: DarkSeoul — the wiper that came before Sony

scenes.label: 2 p.m. in Seoul: the screens die
scenes.narration: [dramatically] At exactly 2 p.m., thousands of computers across South Korea died together. [short pause] [serious] It was Wednesday, March 20, 2013. Banks and TV stations froze. Machines restarted and never came back. One reporter photographed a dead screen. It said, Boot device not found. [curious] Someone had set a timer. But who? To find out, we go back almost a year.

scenes.label: A country that lives online
scenes.narration: [calmly] South Korea was one of the most connected countries on Earth. People paid with cards and banked on their phones. Big banks like Shinhan and NongHyup handled their money. TV networks like KBS and MBC told them the news. All of it ran on computers. [ominously] And investigators say someone across the border was planning to hit them.

scenes.label: June 2012: the quiet start
scenes.narration: [curious] South Korean investigators later blamed North Korea. They say the planning began in June 2012. Nobody in Seoul noticed. Workers got emails that looked normal. They were bait. Security company McAfee found emails like these planted back doors. A back door is a secret way into a computer. [whispers] The attackers were inside, and they were waiting.

scenes.label: A dangerous winter and a timer
scenes.narration: [serious] Then came early 2013, and tensions rose. In February, North Korea tested a nuclear weapon. It also said the 1953 deal that stopped the Korean War no longer counted. That same month, investigators say, the attackers ran a test. Like a fire drill. [short pause] Then someone set the timer. March 20. 2 in the afternoon.

scenes.label: The safety tool that turned
scenes.narration: [cautiously] But how do you hit thousands of computers at once? The attackers found a shortcut. Big companies use special software to send updates to all their computers. At some places, that software came from AhnLab, a Korean security company. The attackers used stolen usernames and passwords to get in. [short pause] The tool meant to keep computers safe now carried the bomb.

visuals.text: login admin; password hidden; access granted

scenes.label: 2 p.m.: the wipe begins
scenes.narration: [dramatically] March 20. The clock hit 2. The timer went off. [short pause] The program was a wiper. It doesn't steal. It destroys. It erased the part of a hard drive that tells a computer how to start. Without that, the machine is a dead box. Researchers at Sophos found it wrote one strange word over and over. Hastati. It's the name of an ancient Roman army unit.

scenes.label: Frozen ATMs, dark newsrooms
scenes.narration: [worried] Out on the streets, people felt it fast. At Shinhan Bank, online banking and ATMs went down for about two hours. At one Starbucks in downtown Seoul, customers had to pay cash. Inside the TV stations, staff at KBS, MBC and YTN couldn't log in to their news systems. [short pause] Oddly, the shows stayed on the air. [nervous] But who was behind it?

visuals.text: login KBS; login MBC; login YTN; access denied

scenes.label: Skulls on the homepage
scenes.narration: [curious] That afternoon, a strange clue popped up. The website of LG U+, a big Korean internet company, was taken over. It showed skulls and played laughter. A group called the Whois Team claimed it. Their message said, [softly] This is the beginning of our movement. [short pause] Unfortunately, we have deleted your data. [serious] It looked like a prank. It wasn't.

visuals.text: This is the beginning of our movement. - Whois Team
We have deleted your data. - Whois Team

scenes.label: 48,000 computers wiped
scenes.narration: [serious] Over the next days, the damage grew clearer. First, officials counted about 32,000 broken computers. In the end, they said 48,000 computers and servers were hit. That's more than the seats in Yankee Stadium. Some banks struggled for two to five days. [short pause] But officials said no bank records or personal data were taken. [slowly] This attack wasn't about money. It was about chaos.

scenes.label: The China clue that wasn't
scenes.narration: [nervous] Everyone wanted a name. On March 21, South Korea's internet regulator said the bad code came from an address in China. Then officials took it back. The address belonged to NongHyup Bank's own network. [sighs] Clues can lie. And the attackers weren't done. On March 25 and 26, a second wave hit dozens of servers and websites. [curious] Investigators found more than 1,000 internet addresses in 40 countries. So where did it start?

scenes.label: April 10: Seoul names a suspect
scenes.narration: [serious] On April 10, 2013, South Korean officials faced reporters. They named North Korea. They said a spy agency run by the North's military was behind it. Many of the harmful programs had been used before. And North Korean systems had reached into South Korean networks at least 13 times. Chun Kil-soo, from Korea's internet security agency, said, [slowly] We saw evidence that the attack was extremely carefully prepared.

scenes.label: Years in the shadows
scenes.narration: [curious] Security companies kept digging. Symantec named the hackers the DarkSeoul gang. It tied them to about four years of attacks on South Korea. One hit came on June 25, 2013, the anniversary of the start of the Korean War. McAfee found spying on South Korea's military going back to at least 2009. [ominously] The wipe was just the loud part.

scenes.label: The road to Hollywood
scenes.narration: [deep voice] Now jump ahead to November 2014. Sony Pictures, the Hollywood studio, was hacked. On December 19, the FBI blamed North Korea. And it pointed back to Seoul. It said the Sony tools were like those used in March 2013 against South Korean banks and TV stations. [short pause] In 2016, security companies tied both attacks to one team. Today, it's known as Lazarus.

scenes.label: The warning nobody heard
scenes.narration: [reflective] Here's what makes this chilling. Almost everything in the Sony hack happened in Seoul first. The quiet break-in. The fake hacker group. The skulls on a screen. A timer set to the minute. American expert James Barnett warned, [serious] This needs to be a wake-up call. This can happen anywhere. [long pause] [softly] Most of the world didn't wake up until it hit Hollywood. If you like true stories like this, subscribe to Breach Uncovered.

This can happen anywhere. - James Barnett

facts.claim: Computers at South Korean banks and broadcasters went down at 2 p.m. local time on Wednesday, March 20, 2013.
A KBS World Radio reporter photographed a screen reading 'Boot device not found. Please install an operating system on your hard disk.'
Victims included KBS, MBC, YTN, Shinhan Bank, NongHyup Bank, Jeju Bank and insurance affiliates.
Shinhan Bank had a roughly two-hour shutdown including online banking and ATMs; a downtown Seoul Starbucks asked customers to pay cash; TV broadcasts were not affected.
North Korea had tested a nuclear weapon a month earlier and revoked the 1953 armistice; a defense ministry spokesman said it was premature to blame the North.
LG U+ homepage replaced with skulls, laughter and lightning effects and a Whois Team message 'an interest in hacking' / 'beginning of our movement'.
Whois Team video: 'Unfortunately, We have deleted your data. We'll be back soon.'

Wipers overwrote the MBR with repeated 'HASTATI.' or 'PRINCPES' strings, names of Roman battle-line units; one variant waited until March 20, 2013 14:00; tried to kill AhnLab and Hauri processes; forced reboot; a companion script targeted Linux/Unix servers.
AhnLab ASEC found attackers distributed malware through patch management software.
Spear-phishing emails in the three months before the attack installed back doors (McAfee).
Initial estimate about 32,000 computers; later 48,000 PCs and servers.

Banks hampered two to five days; broadcasters' staff couldn't access news systems for several days; no bank records or personal data compromised; 76 malware programs, 30 recycled; 1,000+ IPs in 40 countries; planned about eight months; quote 'extremely carefully prepared'.
On March 21, 2013 the Korea Communications Commission traced code to a Chinese IP; later retracted as a NongHyup private IP address.

Second wave March 25-26 targeted 58 servers and 14 websites including North Korean defector sites; planning from June 2012; February 2013 test; 13 direct accesses from North Korean systems; Reconnaissance General Bureau methods.
South Korea announced North Korea attribution on April 10, 2013.
Symantec tied the DarkSeoul gang to about four years of attacks, including a June 25, 2013 DDoS on the 63rd Korean War anniversary.
McAfee's Operation Troy dates to at least 2009 and aimed to spy on South Korea's military.
FBI on December 19, 2014 said Sony malware was similar to tools used in a March 2013 cyberattack against South Korean banks and media outlets.
Operation Blockbuster (February 2016) linked DarkSeoul and the Sony attack to the Lazarus Group.
James Barnett of Venable: 'This needs to be a wake-up call. This can happen anywhere.'
Malware was spread through AhnLab's enterprise patch management software at some targeted sites, using stolen legitimate usernames and passwords; some systems carried a logic bomb set for March 20.
Chun Kil-soo of the Korea Internet Security Agency: 'We saw evidence that the attack was extremely carefully prepared.'
Operation Blockbuster (announced February 25, 2016) connected malware used in Operation DarkSeoul and Operation Troy to the Lazarus Group, believed to be behind the 2014 Sony Pictures attack.
Yankee Stadium seats about 46,500 people, fewer than the 48,000 machines hit.

seo.youtube_description:
How South Korea was hacked: the true story of DarkSeoul, the cyberattack that wiped 48,000 computers at banks and TV stations at exactly 2 p.m. on March 20, 2013.
It looked like a prank. It was months in the making, and it was a warning before the Sony Pictures hack.

On March 20, 2013, ATMs froze in Seoul and newsrooms at KBS, MBC and YTN went dark. A group calling itself the Whois Team put skulls on an internet company's homepage. But investigators found something far bigger: planning that started in June 2012, fake emails that opened secret back doors, and a trusted software-update tool turned into a delivery truck for a timed wiper.

In April 2013, South Korea blamed North Korea's military spy agency. Researchers later tied the DarkSeoul gang to years of attacks. In December 2014, the FBI pointed back to this attack when it blamed North Korea for hacking Sony Pictures. This hacking documentary tells the whole story in plain English, using only public records and news reports.
